--- title: "Direct sampling & plots" sidebar: start --- ## Sample distribution Every distribution in `m.dist` can be sampled **directly**, outside of a model, by passing `sample=True`. This is useful for prior predictive checks, simulating data, or quickly inspecting a distribution's shape. ::: {#e9ba9a6d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from BayesForge import bf m = bf() # Draw 1000 samples from a standard normal m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(4,), sample=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` jax.local_device_count 24 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ```{=html} 
SampledData([ 0.79051853, -1.5325626 , -1.31241422, -0.74232626], dtype=float64)
``` ::: ::: By default (`to_jax=False`) a direct sample is returned as a **`SampledData`** object — a thin wrapper around a JAX array. It behaves like a JAX array everywhere (arithmetic, indexing, `jnp.*` functions, `jit`/`vmap`/`grad`, use as a distribution parameter), and its `repr` reports the dtype so you can see the kind and precision at a glance: The extra thing a `SampledData` gives you over a raw array is a set of **built-in plotting methods** and **built-in helper functions**. If you only want the raw JAX array (no wrapper, no plotting helpers), pass `to_jax=True`: ::: {#ab44c734 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,), sample=True, to_jax=True) # plain jax array ``` ::: ## Plotting helpers Each plotting method is called directly on the sampled object. Most accept `interactive=True` (the default, **Plotly**) or `interactive=False` (**matplotlib / seaborn**): The available methods depend on the **shape** of the sampled array. ### 1D-(n_samples,) ::: {.panel-tabset} #### histogram ::: {#8c51cf35 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,), sample=True).hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### kernel ::: {#5307f801 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,), sample=True).density() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### PPC ::: {#7430e77d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0,1,shape=(100,4),sample=True).ppc_plot(m.dist.normal(0,1,shape=(100,),sample=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### Time series — `(n_samples, n_time)` Treat the second axis as time and summarise across draws. ::: {#5b0853ae .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.gaussian_random_walk(scale=0.5, num_steps=50, shape=(500,), sample=True).timeseries(credible_interval=0.9) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: ### 2D-(n_samples, n_variables) ::: {.panel-tabset} #### histogram ::: {#112694b1 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### kernel ::: {#599335e1 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).density() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### boxplot ::: {#523b47d6 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### violinplot ::: {#d7ab0bd2 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).violinplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### pairplot ::: {#4a4468d4 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).pairplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### corr_heatmap ::: {#74e58a66 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.lkj_cholesky(4, 2, name = 'a', sample = True).corr_heatmap() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### traceplot ::: {#396105a4 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).traceplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### surface_3d Computes a 2D Kernel Density Estimate (KDE) using the first two variables. It plots a 3D surface where the X and Y axes represent the variables and the Z axis represents the estimated probability density. ::: {#f2a711d2 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).surface_3d() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### scatter3d Takes the first three variables (columns) and plots them directly as points in a 3D space (X, Y, and Z axes). Requires the array to have at least 3 variables (columns). ::: {#d3484dad .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4), sample=True).scatter3d() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### Posterior predictive Compare draws against observed data. ::: ### 3D-(n_samples, n_groups, n_times) ::: {.panel-tabset} ::: {#297520f9 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0, 1, shape=(1000,4, 3), sample=True).hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: #### 3D scatter — `(n_samples, >=3)` ::: {#8dc918a7 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape=(100,4, 5), sample = True).hist() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: ## Non-plot helper In addition to plot helper functions, there are several other helper functions that can be used to compute summaries or transform the sampled array. For reduction operations (like `mean`, `std`, `sum`), you can pass an `axis` argument to reduce along specific dimensions. For example, passing `axis=0` will reduce across the sample dimension. ### mean ::: {#aa3b7b3b .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} m.dist.normal(0,1, name = 'a', shape=(100,4), sample = True).mean(axis=0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=59} ```{=html}
